definitions.P: number of passes = number of maximal rotation runs = (#joints) + 1
definitions.e_h: number of times hexagon h is entered = number of passes lying in h
definitions.G: multiplicity excess := P - n!/n = sum_h (e_h - 1); every hexagon is entered at least once and sum_h e_h = P, and there are n!/n hexagons
definitions.F: abandonment count.  At a joint leaving the pass-end word p the legacy engine sets abandonment = NOT visited(sigma(p)): the pass stopped rotating while its rotation successor was still unvisited.  If sigma(p) was already visited the rotation was BLOCKED and it is not an abandonment.
definitions.nu: hexagon-successor permutation on passes (Round 126): nu(p) is the pass whose entry word is sigma^{len(p)}(entry(p)) = sigma(exit(p)); its cycles are exactly the hexagons, with cycle length e_h
definitions.r: number of runs = maximal blocks of consecutive passes in the same orbit
definitions.N: see section 13 - the historical definition S + F - O is the one in question

fg_theorem.abandonment_iff: abandonment(p) <=> p < nu(p) in walk order
fg_theorem.F: F = #{p : p < nu(p)} = number of nu-ascents
fg_theorem.J: J = G - F = sum_h (d_h - 1), d_h = number of nu-descents in hexagon h
fg_theorem.d_h_lower_bound: d_h >= 1 for every hexagon (a full cycle cannot be all ascents)
fg_theorem.m2: e_h = 2 => exactly one of the two passes is an ascent => d_h = 1 => contributes 0
fg_theorem.m3plus: e_h >= 3 => d_h may exceed 1 => J may be positive
fg_theorem.J_positive_requires: some hexagon entered at least THREE times

P.why: sum_h e_h = P over the n!/n hexagons, each entered at least once, so P - n!/n = sum_h (e_h - 1) = G BY DEFINITION; F is the abandonment count and only equals G when every hexagon's nu-cycle has exactly one descent

L.why: L = 725 + (#joints) + S + H and #joints = P - 1 = n!/n - 1 + G

D.why: D := (n-1)O - P with O = O_min + k and P = n!/n + G

N.why: L = 844 + G + S + H must equal 868 + (k + N + H), and G + S = O + N requires N = S + G - O

master.old: L = 867 + k + F + e + x + H - f_out
master.corrected: L = 867 + k + G + e + x + H - f_out
master.why: S = (r-1) + x - f_out is F- and G-free; substituting into L = L_base + G + S + H gives the G form

theorem_A.old: O <= 1 + S + F   <=>   f_out <= F + e + x
theorem_A.corrected: O <= 1 + S + G   <=>   f_out <= G + e + x
theorem_A.why: the algebraic equivalence uses S = (r-1) + x - f_out and r = O + e, so O <= 1 + S + X  <=>  f_out <= X + e + x for any X; the SLAB derivation needs the version whose X matches the length identity, i.e. G.  The F-version is strictly STRONGER (F <= G) and is NOT what the table needs.
theorem_A.note: the two coincide exactly when J = 0

slab.old: k + H <= 4 from S >= O - 1 - F and F + S + H <= 27
slab.corrected: k + H <= 4 from S >= O - 1 - G and G + S + H <= 27
slab.why: both substitutions cancel the G, so the BOUND k + H <= 4 is unchanged - only its derivation is relabelled

cells.why: the row bound is G <= (n-1)k from D >= 0 and the column bound is k <= 4 from k + H <= 4; both are statements about G

slab_table.exhaustive: every walk has a well-defined (k, G), so the decomposition is exhaustive; the FINITENESS (k <= 4) still rests on Theorem A, which is proved only for G <= 2

j_cost_theory.J: J = sum_h (d_h - 1), d_h = number of nu-descents in hexagon h
consequences: J <= G - m, hence F = G - J >= m: the abandonment count is at least the number of multiply-entered hexagons
J > 0 requires some hexagon entered at least THREE times
G = 2 with two doubled hexagons (m = 2) => J <= 0 => F = 2
G = 2 with one tripled hexagon (m = 1) => J <= 1, so F in {1, 2}
j_cost_theory.salvage: in the G <= 1 regime - which is exactly what every engine from Round 115 through Round 125 searched - J is identically zero, so F = G there and no result is affected by the collision beyond its NAME
j_cost_theory.no_length_cost: J does not appear in L = L_base + G + S + H, so a unit of J costs no length by itself; the salvage comes from the multiplicity requirement e_h >= 3, not from a length penalty

step_6.statement: 'extra hexagon entries arise exactly one per abandonment, hence P = 120 + F'
step_6.what_is_true: P - 120 = sum_h (e_h - 1) = G BY DEFINITION; the identification of that count with the abandonment count F is what fails
step_6.when_it_holds: exactly when every hexagon's nu-cycle has one descent, i.e. J = 0; automatic when every e_h <= 2
step_6.how_it_was_checked: on 5 concrete strings, all of which happen to have J = 0 (the 872 witness has F = G = 25, the greedy 873 has F = G = 0), so the error was invisible

step_7_8.statement: L = 844 + F + S + H and L = 868 + (k + N + H)
step_7_8.status: inherits the step-6 error - both need G in place of F

round_127_salvage.corrected_name: Theorem 127.1 (two doubled hexagons) - a LOCAL MULTIPLICITY lemma
round_127_salvage.statement: let h and g be two distinct hexagons each entered exactly twice; if all four of their passes exit by a free (omega = 2) arc, then at least two orbits carry an extra run, i.e. e >= 2
round_127_salvage.why_it_survives: the proof only uses: the nu-cycle structure on the passes of a hexagon, the order lemma, the uniqueness of a run's first pass, and the fact that a hexagon's n words lie in n distinct orbits. None of these mentions abandonment or the multiplicity excess total, so the proof is untouched by the F/G collision.

f0_audit.question: is F = 0 => G = 0?
f0_audit.proof: a hexagon with e_h >= 2 has at least one nu-ascent, and an ascending pass can never be the walk's last pass (nothing follows it), so it really contributes an abandonment; hence G >= 1 => F >= 1
f0_audit.classification: Round 115 SURVIVES unchanged - G = 0 and F = 0 are the same set

f1_audit.question: is F = 1, G > 1 possible?
f1_audit.answer: YES in general - 46 of the 29,255 legal n = 4 walks have F = 1, G = 2, all with multiplicity partition (2,) i.e. ONE hexagon entered three times
f1_audit.but: those walks have P = 122, not 121, so they were never in any engine's domain; in the corrected (k, G) parameterisation they live in the G = 2 column, which is OPEN and was never claimed closed
f1_audit.conclusion: no walk escapes the table - the (k, G) decomposition is exhaustive
